questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes sensation from perception?
options: Sensation detects stimuli; perception gives them meaning
Sensation gives stimuli meaning; perception detects them
Sensation happens in the brain; perception happens in the eye
Sensation is learned; perception is entirely inborn in humans
questions.explanation: Sensation is the detection of physical energy by sense receptors and its conversion into neural impulses. Perception is the brain's process of selecting, organising and interpreting that information.

questions.stem: In the visual system, transduction is the process of:
options: sending impulses along the optic nerve to the brain
organising features into a meaningful whole object
converting light energy into neural impulses
focusing light onto the retina at the back of the eye
questions.explanation: Transduction occurs when photoreceptors (rods and cones) in the retina convert light energy into electrochemical neural impulses. Focusing light is part of reception.

questions.stem: Neural impulses travel from the retina along the optic nerve towards the primary visual cortex. This stage is called:
options: transmission
reception
transduction
interpretation
questions.explanation: Transmission is the sending of neural impulses from the retina via the optic nerve, through the thalamus, to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the stages of visual perception?
options: reception, transduction, selection, transmission, interpretation, organisation
reception, transduction, transmission, selection, organisation, interpretation
reception, transmission, transduction, organisation, selection, interpretation
transduction, reception, transmission, selection, interpretation, organisation
questions.explanation: Light is received and focused, transduced into neural impulses, transmitted to the visual cortex, where features are selected, then organised into patterns and finally interpreted.

questions.stem: Feature detectors in the visual cortex respond to specific features such as lines at certain angles. These operate in which stage of perception?
options: interpretation
selection
reception
organisation
questions.explanation: In selection, feature detector cells in the primary visual cortex respond to particular features such as edges, angles and movement. These features are then organised into wholes.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the two types of photoreceptor in the retina?
options: Rods work best in dim light; cones detect colour and fine detail
Cones work best in dim light; rods detect colour and fine detail
Rods and cones both detect colour equally well in very dim light
Rods are found mainly in the fovea, where vision is the sharpest
questions.explanation: Rods are very sensitive to light and support vision in dim conditions but do not detect colour. Cones, concentrated in the fovea, detect colour and fine detail in bright light.

questions.stem: After a few minutes in a room, a student stops noticing the hum of a fridge and the feel of her watch. This is an example of how sensation acts as a data-reduction system through:
options: size constancy
retinal disparity
sensory adaptation
perceptual set
questions.explanation: Sensory adaptation is a reduced response to an unchanging stimulus, which frees attention for new information. Thresholds, attention and feature detection also reduce the amount of data processed.

questions.stem: The Gestalt principle of figure-ground refers to the tendency to:
options: fill in gaps so that incomplete shapes look whole
group together objects that look similar to each other
group together objects that are near one another
separate a scene into an object and its background
questions.explanation: Figure-ground organisation separates what stands out (the figure) from the surroundings (the ground). Filling gaps is closure, and grouping similar or nearby objects is similarity or proximity.

questions.stem: A logo made of separate dots arranged in a circle is seen as a complete circle. Which Gestalt principle is this?
options: figure-ground
proximity
closure
similarity
questions.explanation: Closure is the tendency to fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole figure. The gaps between the dots are ignored and a circle is seen.

questions.stem: In a grid of dots, rows of red dots alternate with rows of blue dots, and the grid is seen as rows rather than columns. Which principle explains this?
options: similarity
proximity
closure
continuity
questions.explanation: Similarity is the tendency to group elements that share features such as colour or shape. The dots are evenly spaced, so proximity cannot explain the rows.

questions.stem: Two lines cross to form an X, and we see two straight lines rather than two V shapes meeting at a point. Which principle is this?
options: continuity
closure
similarity
figure-ground
questions.explanation: Continuity (good continuation) is the tendency to perceive smooth, continuous lines and patterns rather than abrupt changes in direction.

questions.stem: As a friend walks away from you, her image on your retina gets smaller, but you do not perceive her as shrinking. This is:
options: brightness constancy
linear perspective
size constancy
shape constancy
questions.explanation: Size constancy is perceiving an object as staying the same size despite changes in the size of its retinal image. Linear perspective is a depth cue.

questions.stem: A door opening towards you casts a trapezoid-shaped image on your retina, yet you still see it as rectangular. This is:
options: interposition
shape constancy
size constancy
brightness constancy
questions.explanation: Shape constancy is perceiving an object as keeping its shape even when the angle of view changes the shape of the retinal image.

questions.stem: A white shirt in shade reflects less light than a grey shirt in full sun, but the white shirt is still seen as white. This is because brightness constancy depends on:
options: the proportion of light reflected compared with its surroundings
the total amount of light the shirt reflects into the eye
the size of the image of the shirt on the retina of the eye
the angle from which the shirt is being viewed at that time
questions.explanation: Brightness constancy keeps perceived brightness stable because the brain compares how much light an object reflects relative to nearby surfaces, rather than the absolute amount.

questions.stem: Of these depth cues, which one only works when a person views a scene with two eyes?
options: linear perspective
interposition
texture gradient
retinal disparity
questions.explanation: Retinal disparity is a binocular cue: each eye sees a slightly different image, and the brain uses the difference to judge depth. The others are monocular pictorial cues.

questions.stem: When you focus on a finger moving towards your nose, your eyes turn inwards, and muscle feedback signals that the object is close. This depth cue is:
options: accommodation
retinal disparity
height in the visual field
convergence
questions.explanation: Convergence is the binocular cue in which the eyes turn inwards to focus on close objects, with kinaesthetic feedback from the eye muscles signalling distance. Accommodation is the change in the shape of the lens.

questions.stem: Accommodation is a depth cue that involves:
options: the brain comparing the two slightly different images
nearer objects partly blocking the view of further ones
the lens changing shape to focus on near or far objects
the eyes turning inwards to focus on an object up close
questions.explanation: Accommodation is a monocular physiological cue: the ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens, becoming thicker for near objects, and feedback from these muscles helps judge distance.

questions.stem: In a painting, a road's edges come together towards the horizon. Which pictorial depth cue is used?
options: interposition
relative size
linear perspective
texture gradient
questions.explanation: Linear perspective is the apparent convergence of parallel lines as they recede into the distance. Texture gradient is the change from coarse to fine detail with distance.

questions.stem: A photo of a pebbly beach shows clear, separate pebbles in front and an increasingly fine, smooth surface further away. This cue is:
options: texture gradient
linear perspective
relative size
height in the visual field
questions.explanation: Texture gradient is the change in detail from coarse and distinct nearby to fine and dense in the distance. Gibson saw it as a key source of depth information in the environment.

questions.stem: In a picture, one tree partly blocks the view of a house, so the tree is seen as closer. This depth cue is:
options: convergence
interposition
accommodation
relative size
questions.explanation: Interposition (overlap) is the cue that an object partly covering another is closer. Accommodation and convergence are physiological cues, not pictorial ones.

questions.stem: Gregory (1970) argued that perception is a top-down process in which:
options: the light reaching the eye contains all the information needed
perception is fixed at birth and unaffected by experience
the eye alone interprets objects before signals reach the brain
the brain forms and tests hypotheses using past knowledge
questions.explanation: Gregory saw perception as hypothesis testing: sensory information is often incomplete, so the brain uses stored knowledge and expectations to make the best guess about what is being seen.

questions.stem: Gibson's (1966) theory of direct perception proposes that:
options: perception depends mainly on expectations formed through past experience
the brain makes and tests hypotheses about stimuli before perceiving them
perception is a cycle in which schemata direct what we look for next
the optic array holds enough information to perceive the world directly
questions.explanation: Gibson argued perception is bottom-up: the patterns of light in the environment, such as texture gradients and optic flow, directly provide the information needed, without the need for hypotheses.

questions.stem: A driver at night briefly sees a dark shape on the road and perceives it as a dog, but closer up sees it is a bag. Which theory best explains the first, incorrect perception?
options: Gregory's top-down theory, because limited information led to a wrong hypothesis
Gibson's bottom-up theory, because the optic array gave complete information
Gestalt closure, because the bag's outline was filled in to make it complete
Size constancy, because the bag looked the same size at different distances
questions.explanation: In poor viewing conditions sensory data are incomplete, so the brain relies on expectations and forms a hypothesis that may be wrong. Gibson's theory works best in good conditions with rich information.

questions.stem: Which finding most supports Gibson's theory rather than Gregory's?
options: Illusions trick people because they apply the wrong expectations
People see ambiguous figures differently depending on context
Hungry people are quicker to notice pictures of food items
Newborn animals avoid drops before they have learned about heights
questions.explanation: Avoiding drops without prior learning suggests depth information can be picked up directly from the environment. Illusions, context effects and motivation effects all show top-down influences, supporting Gregory.

questions.stem: Neisser's (1976) analysis-by-synthesis model is described as interactionist because it:
options: relies only on information in the light, with no role for memory
relies only on expectations, with no role for sensory information
explains perception as the result of reinforced visual responses
combines bottom-up sensory data and top-down schemata in a cycle
questions.explanation: In Neisser's perceptual cycle, schemata direct exploration, exploration samples information from the environment, and that information modifies the schemata. Both top-down and bottom-up processes contribute.

questions.stem: In Neisser's perceptual cycle, a hiker expects to see a track marker, scans the trees and finds a sign that is a different colour from what she expected. What happens next?
options: Her perception stops because the information conflicts with memory
Her expectation overrides the sign, so she sees the colour expected
Her eyes adapt so that the new colour no longer reaches her brain
Her schema is modified, which changes what she looks for next
questions.explanation: In the cycle, sampled information modifies the schema, and the updated schema then directs further exploration. Perception is continuous and changes as new information arrives.

questions.stem: In visual perception, the term perceptual set refers to:
options: the range of light wavelengths that the eye can detect
a readiness to perceive a stimulus in a particular way
the set of visual receptors found in the retina of each eye
a fixed sequence of stages through which perception passes
questions.explanation: Perceptual set is a predisposition or expectation to perceive something in a certain way, shaped by factors such as context, past experience, motivation, emotion and culture.

questions.stem: The same ambiguous symbol is read as the letter B in a row of letters and as the number 13 in a row of numbers. Which factor influencing perceptual set does this show?
options: context
emotion
motivation
culture
questions.explanation: Context is the setting in which a stimulus appears. The surrounding letters or numbers create an expectation that determines how the ambiguous symbol is interpreted.

questions.stem: Participants who had gone without food for several hours rated pictures of food as brighter than participants who had just eaten. Which factor does this show?
options: motivation
context
past experience
culture
questions.explanation: Motivation, such as hunger, can make people more likely to notice and perceive stimuli related to their needs. Both groups saw the same pictures in the same context.

questions.stem: A person who has just watched a horror film perceives a coat on a door as a figure standing in the dark. Which factor is most likely influencing perception?
options: emotional state
brightness constancy
texture gradient
visual accommodation
questions.explanation: Emotions such as fear can create a perceptual set to see threats, so ambiguous stimuli are interpreted in a threatening way.

questions.stem: People raised in environments with few straight lines and right angles have been found to be less affected by the Muller-Lyer illusion. Which factor in perceptual set does this support?
options: attention
culture
motivation
emotion
questions.explanation: The carpentered world hypothesis proposes that people raised among rectangular buildings learn to read angles as depth cues, making them more prone to the illusion. Culture shapes perceptual experience.

questions.stem: A student focusing on reading her friend's message fails to notice her name being called across the room. This shows that perception is affected by:
options: convergence
shape constancy
transmission
attention
questions.explanation: Attention selects some information for processing while other information is ignored, so unattended stimuli may not be perceived. This shows perception is selective.

questions.stem: Psychologists distinguish a visual illusion from a hallucination. An illusion is:
options: a consistent misperception of a real stimulus
seeing something that is not physically there
a failure of the eye to detect any light
a random error made by one person only once
questions.explanation: An illusion is a consistent misinterpretation of real sensory information, experienced by most people. Seeing something that is not there is a hallucination.

questions.stem: Gregory explained the Muller-Lyer illusion as misapplied size constancy. According to this explanation, the line with outward-pointing fins looks longer because:
options: its fins are grouped by similarity, so they are added to the line's length
its retinal image is larger than the image of the line with inward fins
it resembles the far inside corner of a room, so it is read as further away
it resembles the near outside corner of a building, so it is read as closer
questions.explanation: The outward fins resemble an inside corner receding away from the viewer. The brain treats it as further away and, applying size constancy, enlarges it, even though both lines cast equal images.

questions.stem: In the Ames room, a person standing in one corner looks giant and a person in the other looks tiny. Why?
options: The room's walls use similarity, so the people are grouped with the walls
The room is lit unevenly, so one person reflects more light to the eye
The brain assumes the room is rectangular, so both people seem equally distant
The two people are really very different heights from each other
questions.explanation: The Ames room is trapezoidal but looks rectangular from the viewing point. Assuming a normal room, the brain treats both people as the same distance away and attributes the difference in image size to their height.

questions.stem: Why do illusions such as the Muller-Lyer persist even when we know the lines are equal?
options: Some perceptual processes are automatic and not changed by knowledge
Knowledge always changes perception once it is learned and understood
The eye sends incorrect impulses that the brain cannot then detect
Illusions are learned responses that are reinforced by each viewing
questions.explanation: Knowing the lines are equal does not stop the illusion, which suggests that some perceptual processes operate automatically. This is a challenge for a purely top-down account.
